config.why: Diversification removes only idiosyncratic risk; the systematic component survives any number of holdings — which is why CAPM pays a premium for market risk alone.

activities.name: feMoneyCloze

config.text: Commercial banks create money when they %%0%% — the loan and the deposit arrive together. Maturity transformation makes bank runs a %%1%% equilibrium, and deposit insurance %%2%% the bad equilibrium by changing the payoffs.
config.hint: Loans create deposits; if everyone expects a run, running first is optimal.

activities.anchor: banks lend out the reserves depositors place with
activities.caption: reserves versus deposits — drag the divider
activities.name: feReservesCompare

config.prompt: Reserves and deposits — drag the divider:

before.label: reserves
before.text: settlement balances between banks, held at the central bank

after.label: deposits
after.text: claims created when a bank lends; the loan and the deposit arrive together

config.why: Lending creates deposits first; the textbook money-multiplier chain of fixed re-lending is not how balance sheets work.

activities.anchor: Worked example: two assets each with volatility 20%
activities.caption: mark the portfolio volatility
activities.name: fePortfolioPlace

config.prompt: Two assets each have 20% volatility, correlation 0.3, held 50/50. Place the portfolio volatility.
config.why: Variance = 0.25×0.04 + 0.25×0.04 + 2×0.25×0.3×0.04 = 0.026, so volatility ≈ 16.1% — four points below either asset alone, with no expected-return sacrifice.

activities.caption: pair each human-capital idea with its meaning
activities.name: feHumanMatch

config.prompt: Pair each human-capital idea with its meaning:

pairs.right: each extra year of schooling is associated with roughly 10% higher earnings
hazardous or disagreeable work pays more, ceteris paribus
your earnings move with your employer, industry and city

config.prompt: A firm is 60% equity at 9% and 40% debt at 5% pre-tax, with a 25% tax rate. What is its WACC?
config.why: 0.6×9 + 0.4×5×(1−0.25) = 5.4 + 1.5 = 6.9%. That is the hurdle rate every investment must beat.
config.context: the tax shield is why the debt term is after-tax

activities.anchor: Production theory supplies the demand side for capital
activities.caption: buy the machine? trace the hurdle
activities.name: feInvestBranch

config.root: A machine costs £100,000 and generates £8,000 a year in perpetuity — an 8% gross return. The firm's WACC is 6.9%. Trace the investment decision.

start.text: Should the firm buy the machine?

choices.label: Yes — the 8% return clears the 6.9% hurdle
choices.feedback: Yes — it adds 1.1 points of value over the cost of capital.

choices.label: No — the payback is over twelve years
choices.feedback: Payback ignores the cost of capital and the cash flows after the payback date.

choices.label: Only if the firm has spare cash
choices.feedback: Financing frictions matter in practice, but the project itself clears the hurdle.

buy.text: Buy it: 8% > 6.9%. A 6% machine would fail the same test, even if its payback looked similar.

payback.text: Payback is an accounting rule, not a value test; the project clears the risk-adjusted cost of capital.

choices.label: So buy it?
choices.feedback: Yes — the hurdle is the test.

cash.text: Cash-poor firms may invest less even at identical opportunities — a financing friction, not a verdict on the project.

config.why: Investment stops where the marginal product of capital falls to its cost; irreversibility and financing frictions are the real-world refinements.

activities.anchor: The unit's MR = MC rule survives intact in finance
activities.caption: economic profit, in order
activities.name: feProfitOrder

config.prompt: Put the economic-profit calculation in order:
items: Start with accounting profit — say £12 million on £100 million of capital
Subtract the opportunity cost of the capital employed: 8% × £100m = £8 million
A sister division earning £12m on £200m of capital destroys £4 million
Growth can therefore be value-destroying even at full accounting profitability
config.why: Economic profit charges for the capital employed; that is why the WACC, not the quoted loan rate, is the relevant marginal cost.

config.prompt: Find the line where the market-microstructure reasoning goes wrong:
lines: Exchanges run limit order books where market makers quote bids and asks.
The bid-ask spread is the price of immediacy, and depth is the price of size.
Because liquidity is supplied by competitive firms, it is always available when needed.
On 6 May 2010 the US equity market fell about 9% in minutes as liquidity withdrew.
Market design — circuit breakers, tick sizes, latency rules — is a live research agenda.
config.correction: Liquidity can vanish exactly when it is needed — that is the flash crash's lesson.
config.why: The market is an engineered institution whose rules decide whether it aggregates information or amplifies panic.

activities.caption: true or false — factors and efficiency
activities.name: feFactorJudge

statements.s: CAPM predicted that only market beta earns a premium, but small and value stocks earned too much.
statements.why: The anomaly forced the Fama–French size and value factors into the model.

statements.s: Most of the hundreds of factors in the factor zoo survived out-of-sample replication.
statements.why: Many failed out of sample — asset pricing had its own replication crisis.

statements.s: The efficient-markets hypothesis can be tested only jointly with a model of expected returns.
statements.why: That joint hypothesis problem is why Fama and Shiller could share a Nobel while disagreeing.

statements.s: Efficient markets means prices are always right.
statements.why: Informational efficiency is about speed and competition, not correctness; prices can sit far from fundamentals for years.
